note: W1-LIBRARY round 3. The trade's quarrels: a buckler school and a great-shield carrier who each think the other has given up the point of a shield; a compiler and a rice-cutter arguing about whether a reaping blade was ever a weapon; two curved blades from one coast that are opposite weapons; a smith who thinks the flail is uncivilised and a quay serjeant who thinks that is the merit of it; and a Bravil romance that is wrong about every single thing in the province and right about the weapon, answered by a cohort clerk who cannot stop quoting it. Four declared contradictions land here, two of them closing edges opened in the-arms-of-the-province. Three books are wrong on purpose.

books.title: The Buckler and the Hand: A Course of Instruction for the Lilmoth Yards, With a Word About the Door-Carriers
books.author: Vaneia Corr, who keeps the yard behind the rope-walk at Lilmoth and takes 9 pupils at a time and no more
books.unreliability: The best practical instruction in the library and the nastiest few paragraphs in it. Her method is sound and tested and she teaches it generously; her account of what the great shields are for is a caricature she has never checked against anyone who carries one, and the sneer at the end is the tell that she knows it.

contradicts.on: whether a shield that cannot parry is worth carrying

books.text:
Nine pupils. No more, and no exceptions, and I will not teach anybody's son as a favour. A yard with 20 in it is a place where 20 people learn to do a thing slightly wrong and then confirm it to each other.

THE FIRST WEEK. NOTHING BUT STANDING.

You will hold the buckler out at arm's length, in the fist, knuckles forward, for as long as I say, every day, and you will do nothing else for a week. Pupils leave in the first week. Good.

The reason is that a buckler is not carried on the arm. It has no straps and it is not strapped to anything. It is a fist with a plate in front of it, and everything the school does afterwards depends on your understanding, in the shoulder and not in the head, that the shield goes where your hand goes and your hand goes where you send it.

A strapped shield is a piece of armour that happens to be movable. A buckler is a hand that happens to be armoured. Those two things are not the same trade and a pupil who arrives from a garrison takes 2 months to unlearn the difference.

THE SECOND THING. THE PLATE IS SMALL AND YOU MUST STOP WANTING IT TO BE BIG.

A buckler covers about as much as a supper dish. That is the whole of it and no amount of wishing will widen it.

New pupils spend a month trying to hide behind it. You cannot hide behind it. Stop. What it covers is not your body; what it covers is the *line* between the point of his weapon and any part of you, and a plate the size of a supper dish held out at arm's length, close to his point rather than close to your chest, covers a cone that widens all the way back to you.

Out. Always out. A buckler held at the chest is a decoration. A buckler held out at the length of the arm, moving as little as possible, is a wall with a hole in it that he cannot find.

THE PARRY, WHICH IS THE WHOLE SCHOOL.

Blocking is what you do when the parry has failed. I teach it, because it happens, and because a pupil who has been taught only the clever thing dies the first time the clever thing does not come off.

But: the buckler exists in order to parry, and a parry is the only defence in the province that costs the other man something.

A block takes the blow. It stops there. You are unhurt, he is unhurt, you are both where you were, and he has the next move because he chose the last one. A block is a way of not losing.

A parry does not take the blow. It meets the blow moving, on the flat, at an angle, and turns it off its line, and because he had committed his weight to a line that has now gone somewhere else, he goes with it. For the space of a breath he is a man leaning at nothing with both hands full.

That breath is the whole of what I sell.

HOW IT IS DONE, AND IT IS NOT WHAT PUPILS EXPECT.

Not a swat. Never a swat. A pupil who swats has told me he is thinking about the weapon and not about the man.

The motion is small, it is early, and it is diagonal. Small: a hand's breadth of travel, no more, because a large motion has to be started sooner and can be seen. Early: you meet the blade before it has got its speed up, near his hand rather than near his point. Diagonal: down-and-across, or up-and-across, never straight into it, because straight into it is a block wearing a parry's coat.

And the last part, which nobody writes down and which is why the yards teach in yards. You do not parry the weapon. You parry the *place the weapon is going to be*, and the place the weapon is going to be is decided in his shoulder about a beat before his hand knows about it.

Watch the shoulder. Watch it for 2 years and you will stop having to watch it.

WHAT THIS SCHOOL IS BAD AT, HONESTLY STATED.

Three of them and you will meet all three.

Crowds. A buckler is a duellist's tool and a duel is two people. In a press you cannot see the shoulder you need to see and you cannot reach out with your hand without somebody else's business arriving in it. In a press, take a shield with straps like everybody else and do not be proud.

Heavy weapons. A parry turns a blade aside; it does not turn a falling weight aside. A great-hammer coming down does not have a line to be taken off. It has a place it is going, and the place is through your supper dish, through your fist, and through you. Against the heavy weapons I teach one thing and it is footwork, and the pupils who do not like being told to run away go and learn something else, and they are the ones I read about.

Tiredness. Everything above requires you to be sharp. On the 6th minute of a fight nobody is sharp, and a school built on timing is a school with an hourglass in it.

THE DOOR-CARRIERS.

I am asked about this every intake because one of them has always seen a procession at Helstrom and thought it looked magnificent.

A door is a wall a person has agreed to carry. It cannot parry. It will never parry. Everything I have spent this book describing is unavailable to the person holding one, and what they have instead is a great deal of weight and a great deal of patience.

I will grant the weight is real. Three of them across a channel will stop anything.

But look at what has been given up. The whole of the offensive part of a shield — the moment where his weight goes past you and he is open and he is *yours* — is gone. A door-carrier can never take that moment. They can only refuse yours. A shield that can only refuse is a wall, and a wall does not win, and if you have ever wondered why the great shields only appear in stories where the point is that everybody behind them survived, that is your answer.

They will say to you that not everybody is quick, and that there is a place in a line for somebody who never was, and it is a fine thing to say and I have heard it said very movingly by a large woman at Helstrom.

Here is what I say back. Nobody is born quick. Quick is 4 years in a yard. When they tell you they were never quick what they are telling you is that nobody offered to teach them, and I find it easier to be angry about that than to admire it.

Nine pupils. Come on the first day of the month.

books.title: A Letter to Teeus-Ahai, Who Should Have Asked Somebody Who Cuts Rice
books.author: Ojal-Weeth, rice-cutter at the Lilmoth terraces, dictated to his granddaughter and sent unasked
books.unreliability: He is right about the tool and wrong about what he thinks that settles. He assumes that because a thing is obviously a farm implement it cannot ever have been anything else, which is the same error in the opposite direction from the one he is writing to correct.

contradicts.on: whether the reaping blades were ever weapons before the Duskfall

books.text:
Teeus-Ahai. You do not know me. I have read your book about the long curved blades, or my granddaughter has read it to me twice, and I have been cross for a fortnight and she says I should send this rather than keep saying it at supper.

You have written a careful book. You have asked keepers and you have asked serjeants and you have asked three households at Lilmoth, and you did not ask one person who cuts rice.

I have cut rice for 52 years.

FIRST. WHAT THE BLADE IS.

The harvest edge is a rice hook on a long shaft. That is all. The curve is that shape because rice stands in water and you cut it a hand above the water, and a straight edge at that height either goes into the water or takes the head off, and a curve does neither. The edge is on the inside because you draw it toward you, because the stalk must be gathered before it is cut or you have cut it and it has fallen in the water and you have lost it.

Every single thing you find remarkable about these blades is a thing about rice.

You write that the motion is a full revolution and that the person turns with it and that it comes from a direction the eye cannot choose. Yes. It does. It is a turn because you are working a circle around yourself with your feet in mud, and you cannot walk in mud all day, so you stand in one place and turn and clear what you can reach and then you take a step. One step for every turn. That is a day's work and I have done 30,000 of them.

You write that the reapers have nowhere to stop. Right, and it worries you, and it does not worry us. A cutting stroke that stops is a wasted stroke. You want the blade to come round and keep coming round and go into the next standing rice without you having to start it again, because a man who starts a heavy blade 4,000 times in a day has a shoulder that is finished at 40.

You write that the mire scythes tip downward so that they will bite the earth and have somewhere to stop. That is not why. They tip downward because a scythe was made for dry grass and a dry-grass blade set level in a rice terrace goes into the water, and turning the tang is what a smith does to make a Cyrodiil blade work in a terrace. It is a repair, not a design.

SECOND. WHAT YOU SHOULD HAVE ASKED.

You spent your book asking whether these were weapons before they were duties.

Nobody in a terrace has ever wondered that. Ask any of us and we will tell you it is a rice hook and we will be a bit short with you about it, the way I am being.

THIRD, AND HERE I WILL BE FAIR TO YOU.

You have one thing right and your keepers are wrong to sit on it.

The grown shafts. You noticed that the procession blades at Soulrest are on shafts that were grown and not cut, and you did not make anything of it.

We do not grow shafts for rice hooks. A rice hook is on a cut pole and when it breaks you cut another, and I have gone through more than I can remember. Growing a shaft takes 8 years of somebody bending a tree and paying attention to it, and no household has ever done that for a thing that cuts rice.

So there is a question in your book and it is not the question you asked. It is: who spends 8 years growing a handle for a farm tool, and what did they think they were making.

I do not know. I want to be plain that I do not know and that a rice-cutter has no business guessing.

LAST.

You write that a weapon which cannot be recalled once begun was never going to be popular with people who have to live among each other afterwards.

That is the sentence my granddaughter read out twice because I made her, and it is a good sentence, and it is the only place in your book where you are talking about people and not about objects.

Come to the terraces in the cutting season and I will put one in your hands and you will find out in an hour what 3 keepers could not tell you in a year. Bring boots. You will not keep them.

books.title: Of the Thrusting Swords, Their Use in This Climate, and the Late Unpleasantness at Gideon
books.author: Maestro Lucien Vare, of the salle on Cooper's Row, Gideon, formerly of Wayrest, and he would like that mentioned
books.unreliability: Excellent on the weapon and shameless about the affair. He gives three versions of the duel at the customs house in the space of two pages and each one improves his own conduct, and he has printed all three because he cannot bring himself to cut any of them.
books.text:
A thrusting sword is a machine for arriving first.

Everything else about it — the sweep, the guard, the ornament that has made these weapons fashionable among people who cannot use them — is in service of that one sentence, and a pupil who has understood it has had the best half of my instruction on the first afternoon.

I. THE PRINCIPLE.

Two men stand at some distance. Each may cover that distance with a blade, and whichever blade covers it in less time arrives first, and the man it arrives at has, at that moment, no further opinions.

A cutting sword must travel sideways to gather its force and then travel forward. A thrusting sword travels forward. It is the shortest path between two points and it is quite literally unanswerable if the two men are equal in everything else.

They are never equal in everything else, and the rest of this book is the everything else.

II. THE THREE PATTERNS AND WHAT EACH IS FOR.

*The bog rapier.* Long, light, and made for a floor. It is the finest expression of the principle and it is a poor weapon in this province, and I will say so in print though the man who sells them on Cooper's Row is a friend of mine.

Long means the point is far from the hand and small errors at the hand become large errors at the point. On a boards floor at Wayrest, with your feet where you put them, that does not signify. On a jetty in the wet season, when your back foot has moved 2 inches without consulting you, the point has moved a hand's breadth and the thrust has gone past his ribs into the air behind him, and he is now inside a very long sword with a very short knife, and you are in trouble that no amount of schooling gets you out of.

*The reed estoc.* Shorter, stiffer, no edge at all, made to go through things that a bog rapier bends against. If you must fight men who wear armour, this is your weapon and there is nothing else worth discussing.

*The duelling pick.* And here I must be honest about something the salles do not like to admit. The pick is not a sword and pretends to be one. It has a spike, a short blade, and a hooked beak on the reverse, and it is carried by men who intend the fight to end at close quarters and who have decided in advance that they will not be losing it politely. In a formal meeting it is beneath contempt. In the province, on a stair, at night, it is the weapon I would pick up.

III. THE GUARD, AND THE ONE THING I TEACH THAT THE SCHOOLS AT WAYREST DO NOT.

Point high, held between the eyes and his, hand forward, side on, weight back.

Every school teaches that. Here is the addition.

At Wayrest we hold the point still and let the fight come to us, because a still point is a threat that costs nothing to maintain and because the floor does not move.

In this province I teach the point *low* until the moment of the thrust — down and to the outside, near the hip, the blade almost trailing — and then up and through in one motion.

The reason is mud. A high point requires a still body, and a still body in this country is a body slowly sinking. The low guard lets you keep your feet moving, adjusting, testing what you are standing on, all the way up to the instant of the attack, at the cost of a fraction of a beat in the delivery.

At Wayrest I would be laughed at. At Wayrest I would deserve it. Here I have watched two Wayrest men in 6 years go over backwards without being touched, in front of witnesses, and there is no lesson in a salle that survives sitting down.

IV. THE PARRY, BRIEFLY, BECAUSE VANEIA CORR HAS WRITTEN IT BETTER.

Small, early, diagonal, near his hand. She is right, she teaches it better than I do, and I send pupils across the river to her when they have the hands for it and not the feet.

I will add one thing she leaves out because she teaches the buckler and I teach the sword. When the sword itself is the thing parrying, the parry and the riposte are the same motion or they are two motions and you have lost. Turn his line aside and go up his blade in the same breath. A pupil who parries, admires it, and then thrusts has done two beautiful things too slowly.

V. THE LATE UNPLEASANTNESS AT THE CUSTOMS HOUSE.

I am obliged to address this because it is talked about and because the account being told at the Gideon markets is a slander.

Here is what happened. The factor's man said a thing about my school and about the province and about which of the two was the greater embarrassment. I invited him to withdraw it. He declined. We went out to the yard behind the customs house with two of his people and one of mine, and I put my point through his upper arm on the second exchange, and the matter concluded.

I am aware that a version is circulating in which he slipped. He did not slip. He stepped back onto ground he had not tested and his back foot went into it, and a man whose foot has gone in is a man who must either fall or come forward, and he came forward onto a point I had not moved. That is the province beating a Wayrest education and it is the entire argument of section III of this book.

I should also say, since I have been accused of it, that I did not choose the ground. The ground behind a customs house is the ground behind a customs house. Anyone who imagines I selected a soft patch has a poor opinion of me and a worse one of the yard, which is used for barrels.

To be perfectly frank, and I will put this down because I have gone this far: I knew about the patch. Everybody who drinks at the customs house knows about the patch. It did not occur to me to mention it and I have thought about that since, and I have decided that a man who says a thing like that about a province should find out what the province is like.

VI. FEES.

Ten drakes the month, in advance, and I do not teach anybody who has already killed somebody with a sword, because they have learned the wrong lesson from it and I cannot get it out of them.

books.title: The Reaver and the Sickle: Why Two Curved Blades From the Same Coast Are Not the Same Weapon
books.author: Sees-The-Grain-Turn, who repairs blades at Archon and has been asked this question 400 times
books.unreliability: A repairer's book, which is to say a book about how things break, and it is superb on that and treats every other question as a version of it. She thinks the reaver pattern was copied from the raiders and improved. The raiders think the same about the sickle. Both patterns are older than either story and nobody in the province has the evidence to say so.
books.text:
People bring me two blades and ask me which is better and I have stopped answering, so I have written it down and I keep a copy on the bench and I point at it.

They are both curved. They are both one-handed. They both came off this coast. And they are opposite weapons, and a man who has learned one and picks up the other will be beaten by somebody worse than him.

THE SICKLE.

The naga sickle-blade is a long shallow curve, the belly thin, the point carried well back from the line of the hand.

It sweeps. The whole edge is a cutting edge and the cut happens along the length of it as the blade travels, drawing, the way a knife goes through rope by being pulled and not by being pressed. A sickle stroke that lands and stops has failed. It must keep going.

What that means for the person holding it: your enemy is not a place, he is an arc. You are not aiming at him. You are laying a curve of sharp air through the space he is in and letting his own arrival do half the work.

Reach is its virtue. A sickle held in a low hanging hand covers a width nobody expects, because most of the blade is out to the side of where they are looking.

Where it breaks — and this is my trade so believe me on this if nothing else — it breaks at the point of the belly, on the flat, when somebody has used it to block. They are not made to be hit. A sickle used as a shield comes back to me bent, and a bent one can be straightened twice and after that the steel is tired and will go without warning, and I tell them, and they go away and use it as a shield again.

THE REAVER.

Shorter. Deeper. The belly heavy and dropped forward so the weight sits about two thirds along.

It does not sweep. It chops. It is a hatchet that happens to have an edge all the way back, and everything about the shape puts mass where the blow lands.

A reaver stroke that lands and stops has done its work. It does not want to keep going. It wants to arrive.

For the person holding it: your enemy is a place. You go to the place. The stroke is short, it is thrown from the elbow and the hip rather than from the shoulder, and it is over sooner than a sickle stroke is halfway.

Where it breaks: at the tang, always, in the handle, from years of shock going back into the grip. A sickle dies at the far end and a reaver dies at the near end and you can tell what a person has been carrying by which repairs they have paid for.

THE THING THEY DO NOT ASK, WHICH IS THE ONLY INTERESTING ONE.

Everyone asks which is better. Nobody asks what happens when one meets the other, and I have watched it perhaps 20 times because Archon is a port and the raiders come ashore.

The sickle wins the first exchange and the reaver wins the third.

The first exchange belongs to reach. The sickle is out further, the arc is wider, and the reaver person has to come through it to get anywhere, and coming through it costs them.

By the third exchange they are close, and close is where the sickle has already spent everything it has. A sweep needs room to draw. A drawing cut at arm's-inside distance is a shove with a sharp thing. The reaver at that distance is doing precisely what it was made for, from the elbow, in a space the size of a boat.

So: which is better depends on whether you can keep him out, and that depends on the ground, and the ground in this province is almost never a place where anybody can keep anybody out.

That is the honest answer and nobody likes it and they go and buy whichever one they were going to buy.

ON WHERE THEY CAME FROM, AND I AM AWARE THIS IS DISPUTED.

The reaver pattern is a raider's blade and the raiders have been coming to this coast since before Archon had a wall. My grandfather held that our sickle is the older thing and that the raiders took the curve off us and shortened it because they fight on boats, and that is what I was taught, and that is what I have repeated at this bench for 30 years.

I have met three raiders who told me the reverse with the same confidence, and one of them had a very old blade, and I looked at it for a long time.

I have no way to settle it. A blade does not carry a date. What I can say is that both patterns are made by people who solved a problem, and that the problems were different, and that neither is a bad copy of the other, and if you take nothing else from this bench take that.

CARE, WHICH IS THE PART NOBODY READS.

Both of them rust here in a night. Oil, every day, whether it has been out of the sheath or not. A sheath of untreated hide will rot your blade faster than the air will.

Never sharpen a sickle on a flat stone. The curve wants a round one and a flat stone will put facets on it and a faceted edge catches instead of drawing, and a sickle that catches is a sickle that has taken your wrist round with it.

Bring them to me before they are bad. Everyone brings them to me after.

books.title: On Bog-Iron, and on the Heads Cast From It, With Notes on Why the Province's Hammers Are Ugly
books.author: Serjo Fals Rethan's smith, name given only as Ivas, at Blackrose, who was told to write it and has
books.unreliability: A smith writing under an employer's instruction and hating it, and the hatred has produced an unusually honest technical book. His metallurgy is sound. His view that Blackrose iron is fit for nothing but weights is a grudge against a supplier he names three times.
books.text:
Serjo Fals Rethan has told me to write down what I know about the metal here for a book he is compiling, and I have said I am a smith and not a writer, and he has said that is the point, so here it is and he may take out what offends him.

WHAT BOG-IRON IS.

It grows. That is the first thing and every armourer from Cyrodiil has to be told it twice.

It comes out of the peat in lumps and nodules, and the people who dig it dig the same beds their grandparents dug, and the beds refill, and nobody here finds this remarkable. In the Empire iron is quarried out of a hill and the hill does not put it back.

It is dirty metal. Full of the ground it came out of. You can work it and you can work it well and I have made good things out of it, but it will never take the edge that a bar of Imperial stock takes, and any smith in this province who tells you otherwise is selling.

WHY THAT MATTERS FOR WEAPONS.

An edged weapon is a wager on the quality of your steel. A sword asks the metal to be hard along a line a hand's breadth deep and to stay hard through a thousand impacts. Dirty metal loses that wager. It chips, it rolls, it goes soft in a place you cannot see until the place opens.

A mace asks nothing of the metal except to be heavy and to stay in one piece.

This is why the province is full of hammers and why the hammers are ugly. Not poverty. Not backwardness, whatever Serjo Rethan's guests say at his table. It is a correct answer to the metal available, arrived at by people who could not afford to be wrong about it.

THE CAST HEAD.

A bog-iron mace head is cast, not forged. Poured into a mould of sand and let cool and knocked out and cleaned up and put on a haft.

Casting is what you do when the metal is too dirty to forge cleanly and when you want 40 of a thing and not one. A village smith can pour 12 heads in a morning. He could not forge 2.

The heads are flanged, which is to say they have ridges standing out from the body, and every apprentice asks why and gets told it is for concentrating the blow, and that is half right. It is for concentrating the blow *and* for not sticking. A smooth heavy head arriving on a helm spreads its force and slides. A flanged one puts it all along a ridge and bites and stays put where it landed. The bite is the whole reason the flange exists and it costs you a little in the pour and it is worth it.

THE HAFT.

Straight, always. Ash where we can get it, marsh-oak where we cannot, and marsh-oak is heavier and duller in the hand and every mace on this coast is on it.

Straight because a mace is a weight arriving from directly above. That is its entire argument. Everything else in the province comes from the side or from the front — the sickle sweeps, the sword thrusts, the axe comes on a slant — and the mace comes down.

Down is the direction a shield is worst at. A shield covers a wedge with the point at the shoulder, and the top edge of that wedge is where its owner has to lift, and lifting is slower and more tiring than turning. A tired man's shield drops a hand's breadth. A mace does not need more than that.

I make the haft the length of the arm from the shoulder to the fingers, and no longer, because the moment you make it longer people start swinging it round instead of bringing it down, and then they have made a bad axe out of a good hammer.

ON THE FLAIL, SINCE HE WILL ASK.

Serjo Rethan will want the flail in the book because he has one on his wall.

A flail is a mace head on a chain. I have made them. I will make them for anyone who pays. And I have never made one for a man I liked without telling him what I am about to write here.

A mace stops when you stop. That is the fundamental civility of the weapon. You may begin a stroke and think better of it, and the weight is on the end of a rigid stick and the stick is in your hand and your hand may be persuaded.

A chain cannot be persuaded. Once the head is moving it will complete its circle and it will complete it whether the thing it meets is his helmet or your knee. Every man I know who has carried one for a season has hit himself with it, and the good ones say so, and the ones who deny it are lying or new.

What it buys you is that it goes round things. A shield does not stop a flail; the head goes past the shield's edge and comes round behind it, and the man is hit while covered, which no other weapon on this coast can do.

So it is a real trade and not a stupid one. Reach round a shield, at the cost of never once being able to change your mind. I would not make that trade. I have made 30 of them.

LAST, AND SERJO RETHAN MAY STRIKE IT.

He buys his bar stock from a factor at Gideon who sells him Imperial iron at 4 times what it is worth and tells him it is Skyrim steel. It is not Skyrim steel. It is Cyrodiil bar with a stamp on it that anybody in the trade can read.

I have told him this 3 times in 6 years. He has told me each time that I do not understand the arrangement.

I understand the arrangement.

books.title: In Defence of the Chain, By One Who Has Carried It Longer Than Anyone Living
books.author: Sabinus Ottren, watch-serjeant of the Gideon quays, 31 years, and he has been asked to stop writing to the Office about this
books.unreliability: He is in love with the weapon and every argument he makes for it is an argument against it that he has turned round. The list of injuries in section 4 is offered as proof of his commitment and reads to any other reader as a coroner's brief.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Argues that the flail's inability to be recalled is a virtue because it removes hesitation. His own list of what the weapon has done to him and to his own men is the counter-argument and he prints it proudly.
books.text:
The smith at Blackrose has written that a mace stops when you stop and that this is the fundamental civility of the weapon, and that a chain cannot be persuaded.

He is right about the mechanics and he has drawn the coward's conclusion from them.

1. WHAT I CARRY AND WHY.

Bog-iron flail. Cast head, a hand's span of chain, ash haft. I have carried one on the Gideon quays for 31 years and I have taken it off exactly twice, both times because a surgeon insisted.

The quays are a particular kind of ground and I want that understood before anyone argues with me from a yard. It is crowded. It is wet. It is at night. The people I take hold of are usually 3 or 4 together and they are usually between crates, and there is no room to swing anything and nowhere to step back to.

Every school in this province teaches its pupils to control the distance. Lovely. Come and control the distance on Number 4 quay at the second hour of the morning with a rope coil behind your heels.

2. THE ARGUMENT ABOUT PERSUASION.

Ivas says a mace may be persuaded halfway through a stroke and a chain may not, and he means that as praise of the mace.

Consider what he is praising. He is praising the ability to change your mind in the middle of hitting somebody.

I have watched men change their minds in the middle of hitting somebody. I have watched it on the quays perhaps 100 times. It happens when they see the other man's face, or when they realise how young he is, or when a thing goes through them that they will not be able to explain afterwards. And what happens next is that the stroke arrives at half force and does nothing at all, and the man they were hitting is now certain that they will not do it, and the whole thing goes badly for everyone including the man who was spared.

A weapon that cannot be recalled has taken that moment away from you. You decide once, at the start, with your whole mind, and then it is out of your hands. I say that is a mercy. I say more people have been hurt on my quays by half-strokes from men who hesitated than were ever hurt by me finishing what I began.

3. WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES, TECHNICALLY, SINCE EVERYONE ONLY WRITES ABOUT THE DANGER.

It goes round.

A shield stops what arrives at it. The head of a flail does not arrive at the shield. It arrives at the shield's edge and the chain bends around it and the head continues into the space behind, which is where the man is. There is no defence against this except distance, and I have already explained about distance on a quay.

The same is true of a raised arm, a doorframe, a crate, and a man holding another man in front of him.

And it is slow to see coming, because the head is not where the haft is pointing. Every fighting man in the province has trained his eye to read a weapon's line from the wielder's hands. A flail has no line. The head is somewhere behind and to the side and it is going somewhere neither of you has entirely decided yet.

4. THE COST, WHICH I WILL SET OUT IN FULL BECAUSE THE OFFICE KEEPS ASKING.

I have been struck by my own weapon: on the left knee, twice, the second time badly; on the back of the head, once, which took me off duty for a month; on the left hand, more times than I have counted, which is why the hand is the shape it is.

Of the men I have trained on the quays, 9 have carried the flail. Two gave it up in the first year. One broke his own wrist with it. One struck a colleague on the shoulder in a scuffle at Number 2 and the man has not had the full use of the arm since, and I signed the return, and I stand by the return, and I have not spoken to either of them since.

Five still carry it. All five are alive. Every one of them has been in situations on those quays where I do not believe a sword would have got them out, and I have said so in writing to the Office, and the Office notes it.

5. WHAT I WOULD SAY TO A YOUNG ONE.

Do not carry this unless you are somewhere you cannot step back.

That is the whole rule and everything else is decoration. In a yard, in a field, on a road, on any ground where you can control the distance, this weapon is a poor joke and the smith is right about it and a man with a spear will kill you at his leisure.

On a quay. In a hold. In a lane 4 paces wide. Between crates at night with 3 of them and one of you.

There, you want a thing that goes round corners and that does not stop, and there is nothing else in this province that does either.

6. TO IVAS AT BLACKROSE.

You have made 30 of them and you say you would not make the trade yourself.

I have carried one of yours for 9 years. It came off a cart at Gideon in a lot of 12 and it has your mark on the flange, and it has never once failed, and the chain has been replaced twice and the head never.

You are a better smith than you are a philosopher. Stay at the bench.

books.title: The Lane-Keeper: A Romance of the Marsh, In Which a Bill-Man of the Ninth Wins the Heart of a Rootkeeper's Daughter
books.author: by the author of *A Lady of the Ashlands* and *The Corsair's Confession*; printed at Bravil and sold at Gideon for 2 drakes
books.unreliability: Everything in it about the province is wrong. Everything in it about the weapon is right, in detail, repeatedly, and the author has plainly stood in a yard with one and has plainly never stood in a marsh. The rootkeeper's daughter is described as having hair.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Sets its whole third act in a hill town in Black Marsh with a bell tower, a cobbled square, autumn leaves and a snowfall. There are no such places and there is no such season, and it has sold better than any true account of the province ever printed.
books.text:
CHAPTER THE NINTH, in which Corvinus holds the lane.

They came up out of the mist in the grey hour, and there were 20 of them, and there was one of him.

Corvinus Vale set his back against the cold stone of the fountain and lowered the Lane-Keeper, and the great hooked blade caught what light there was and threw it back at them, and he thought — as a man will think at such a moment — of the way the bell had sounded over the square that morning, and of Sees-The-Dawn-Rise standing beneath the tower with the autumn leaves going past her, and of what she had not said.

"You cannot hold it," said their captain. "Not alone. Not with a hedging tool."

"It is a bill," said Corvinus.

And then, because there was nothing else to say, and because the fog was coming off the cobbles, he showed them what a bill was for.

*The first man came at the run, and this was his error.* The Lane-Keeper does not answer a running man with its point, for the point is the least of it. Corvinus dropped the head low, below the man's shield, and let him come the last half-pace himself, and then he *sat down into the haul*, both hands, his whole weight going back and down, the way a man hauls a boat up a beach.

The hook took the runner behind the knee. He went over backwards onto the stones with a sound like a dropped ladder and did not rise.

"Low," said Corvinus, to nobody. "And pull."

*The second and third came together, which was cleverer,* and the second had a shield up high against the sweep he expected, and this is the thing the schools of Cyrodiil have never understood about the hooked weapons: a shield lifted is a shield that has left somewhere. Corvinus swept, and the shield came up to meet it, and the sweep was never going to arrive — the sweep was a question — and as the man's arm rose the beak of the Lane-Keeper came back the other way and took him under the ribs where the shield had been a moment before.

The third had time to see it. That was Corvinus's gift to him and he did not want it.

*By the ninth man the fountain was slippery* and Corvinus had begun to feel the ache in his forearms that every bill-man knows and no swordsman ever will, for a bill is 8 feet of ash and every stroke is made from the shoulders and the back, and there is no wristwork in it, and no art, and no cleverness, and a man who fights with one is a labourer with a labourer's tiredness.

He thought again of the bell tower. He thought of the snow that had come early to the hills that year, and of how she had said that in her mother's country there was no snow at all and never had been, and of how he had laughed and had not believed her.

*The captain came last.* Of course he came last. He had a Nord greatsword and he held it in the new way, with his forward hand up on the flat of the blade, and Corvinus knew at once that here was a man who had been taught by somebody.

"You are tired," said the captain.

"I am," said Corvinus. "Come and find out how tired."

They fought the length of the lane and back again. Twice the great blade came round faster than any weapon of that size had a right to come round and twice the Lane-Keeper was somewhere else. Corvinus gave ground — a bill-man must give ground, for the weapon is all reach and no defence, and the moment a man is inside it he may as well be holding a broom —

— and at the third turn Corvinus stopped giving ground and put the butt of the haft into the stones and stepped over it.

The captain had committed. He could not do otherwise; that is the price of the great weapons, and Corvinus had been waiting 9 exchanges for it. The greatsword came down where Corvinus had been. The hook came round where the captain now was. And the whole weight of a labourer's shoulders, and 8 feet of ash, and the accumulated patience of a man who had stood in a second rank behind better men for 14 years, arrived behind the captain's ankle.

The bell rang the hour as he fell.

*She found him at dawn,* sitting with his back against the fountain in the drifting leaves, the Lane-Keeper across his knees, counting the notches he had cut into the haft and finding that there were more of them than he remembered cutting.

"You held it," she said.

"I stood in a narrow place," said Corvinus Vale, "and I did the one thing I know, and I did it 20 times."

And Sees-The-Dawn-Rise, whose grey eyes had never in all that long autumn given anything away, put her small hand upon the ash and said nothing at all, and the snow began to come down over the square.

*(End of Chapter the Ninth. Chapter the Tenth: The Rootkeeper's Wrath.)*

books.title: On the Selling of Romances to Soldiers, With Particular Reference to a Book About a Bill
books.author: Neveni Dals, cohort clerk at Thorn, who has been asked to read it aloud 14 times and is done
books.unreliability: A clerk's complaint that turns halfway through into the best short account in the library of what a weapon actually feels like to carry, and she does not notice the turn. Her contempt for the romance is undercut by her knowing whole passages of it from memory.
books.text:
Someone at Gideon has sold 40 copies of a Bravil romance to this cohort at 2 drakes each and I have been asked to read it aloud in the mess 14 times, and I am the clerk, so here is a clerk's return on it.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT.

There is a bell tower. There is a cobbled square. There are autumn leaves. In the last chapter it snows.

I have served in this province 6 years and I have not seen a cobble, a bell tower, a leaf that fell because of a season, or snow. The rootkeeper's daughter has grey eyes and a small hand and hair, and I would like the author to be brought here and shown a rootkeeper.

The captain of the raiders makes a speech before attacking. In 6 years I have never heard anyone make a speech before attacking. What they do is arrive.

And 20 men do not come at one man in a lane one at a time. They come at him 3 abreast and the whole thing is over in the time it takes to write this sentence, and there is no ninth exchange, and nobody counts notches afterwards because nobody who has done it wants to think about the number.

WHAT IS NOT WRONG WITH IT, AND THIS IS THE ANNOYING PART.

The fighting is right.

I have read it out 14 times in a mess full of men who carry these things and not one of them has laughed at the bill and every one of them has laughed at the snow.

Low, and pull, and sit down into the haul. That is what Ostrey says. That is word for word what Ostrey says, and Ostrey cannot read and has never been to Bravil.

The lifted shield having left somewhere. The sweep that is a question. The butt of the haft into the ground and stepping over it. The forearms going in the fourth minute and no wristwork in any of it. Ostrey put his cup down at that part the first time and said: who wrote this.

So somebody in Bravil has stood in a yard with a bill in their hands, for a long time, with somebody who knew, and then written a book about a province they have never smelled.

WHAT I HAVE DECIDED ABOUT IT.

I think the fighting is the true part because it is the part the author cared about, and the province is the false part because the province was the part that would sell.

There is a thing in it I have not been able to get out of my head and I am going to write it down even though it sits badly beside the snow.

Near the end, the man says he stood in a narrow place and did the one thing he knows and did it 20 times.

I have watched Ostrey drill the second rank for 6 years and the whole of what he teaches is one motion. One. He does it in the morning and he does it in the evening and he shouts the same 3 words. And the men who live are the ones who can do the one thing when they are frightened and tired and it is dark, and the men who die are the ones who tried something.

A Bravil hack got that right in a book with snow in it.

I have put the 40 copies in the stores under Miscellaneous, Printed, and I am not reading it again.
